conversation.content: Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Lindsay, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. Its ten questions help us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and—importantly—any thoughts of self-harm that can creep in during the postpartum year. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll move at your pace. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first question.

*settles into the chair, adjusting a burp cloth draped over one shoulder, eyes a bit puffy from another short night*

Morning... sorry if I seem out of it; the baby finally went down at four, so I maybe got two hours. I’m ready when you are.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*gives a small, tired smile*

Most of the time I can still laugh—like yesterday my husband made a silly face while changing a diaper and I actually giggled—but it feels... muted, I guess? The joy doesn’t last long before I’m back to worrying or just feeling kind of flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs lightly, eyes on the burp cloth I’m twisting in my lap*

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could shower alone—but they’re pretty short-lived. Mostly I just feel... flat? I used to count down to brunch with friends or a new episode of my show; now the days kind of blur together and I can’t really muster that “can’t-wait” feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quiet sigh*

Sometimes—like last night when she wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that made my milk upset her stomach. Or if I snap at my husband for no real reason, I’ll lie there wondering why I can’t just be nicer. It’s not constant, but yeah... every so often I catch myself thinking it must be something I’m doing wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods slowly, bouncing one knee*

Yeah... especially at night. I’ll lie there listening to her breathe and suddenly my heart’s racing, sure something’s wrong even though she’s fine. Or I’ll imagine dropping her, or the stroller tipping, and I have to check three times that the buckle’s clicked. It’s not all day, but it pops up more than I’d like, and half the time there’s no real trigger.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*swallows hard, glancing toward the doorway where the baby monitor sits*

Sometimes... like yesterday in the grocery store. She was asleep in the carrier and suddenly my chest got tight, heart pounding, like I had to get out right then. I left the cart and sat in the car until it passed. It only lasted a few minutes, but it felt like my body was sounding an alarm for no reason at all.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales slowly, rubbing my temples*

Yeah... most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get her down for a nap, and the dishes or laundry just stare at me. Some mornings I look at the mess and think, “Where do I even start?” I’m managing the basics—she’s fed, changed, loved—but anything extra feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*gives a small, weary shrug*

It’s more like I’m so tired my body forgets how to fall asleep. I’ll lie there replaying every little thing—did I burp her long enough, why she cried extra today—and then the clock says 2 a.m. and I’m still wide awake. It doesn’t happen every night, maybe three or four times this week, but when it does I just stare at the ceiling feeling... heavy, I guess.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice drops, eyes fixed on my hands*

I do get waves of it—like this morning when she finally smiled at me and instead of feeling happy I just wanted to cry. It’s not every hour, but yeah... most days there’s this dull sadness that sits in my chest and won’t quite lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shakes head slowly*

Not really... I teared up a couple of times this week, but actual crying? Maybe once, briefly, when I couldn’t get her to latch at 3 a.m. and felt like a lousy mom. It’s rare for me to full-on cry—just this tight throat and a few tears that I wipe away fast.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, eyes widening*

No—never. Even on the worst nights, when I feel overwhelmed, I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again, not disappear.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Identified symptoms / behavioral concerns  
- Persistent low mood, described as “flat,” “muted,” or “dull sadness” present most days  
- Markedly reduced pleasure/anticipation (laughing “doesn’t last,” excitement “short-lived”)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt regarding infant care and partner interactions  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety and nocturnal worry; one episode of sudden panic while shopping  
- Frequent nighttime insomnia with rumination; 3–4 nights/week  
- Feeling “barely treading water,” overwhelmed by routine tasks  
- Episodic tearfulness, but no sustained crying spells reported  

Patterns / risk indicators  
- Meets core mood criteria: anhedonia, sadness, guilt, energy/role impairment  
- Anxiety symptoms (physiologic arousal, intrusive catastrophic thoughts about infant safety) appear equally prominent  
- No current suicidal ideation or self-harm intent; protective factor present  

Screening impression  
Elevated score on depressive spectrum; co-occurring anxiety features. Meets threshold for further clinical evaluation for possible postpartum depression and/or anxiety disorder. Safety risk is low at present (denies self-harm). Recommend formal assessment with standardized tool (EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7) and referral for appropriate maternal mental-health services.
